Elam
ē'lăm
n. (a son of Shem and the nation east of Babylon — the archers of the ancient world, broken by prophecy and promised a restoration)
From Hebrew 'Eylam, probably from a root meaning eternity or hidden time, though the connexion is uncertain; the name is first a person, the eldest son of Shem (Gen 10:22), and then the land his descendants held east of the Tigris.

Biblical Definition

Elam is one of the oldest names in the Bible and one of the last to be spoken over. Its king Chedorlaomer heads the eastern coalition of Gen 14 — “Chedorlaomer king of Elam” (Gen 14:1) — the campaign that carried Lot away and drew Abram out with three hundred and eighteen trained servants, and ended with Melchizedek's bread and wine. Elam is remembered chiefly for the bow: “Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen” (Isa 22:6), and when the LORD pronounces judgment it is the bow He names — “Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might” (Jer 49:35). Isaiah summons them against Babylon alongside Media (Isa 21:2). What makes Elam remarkable among the oracles against the nations is the ending. Jeremiah's judgment on Elam does not conclude in desolation but in a promise: “But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the LORD” (Jer 49:39). And in Act 2 the list of nations that heard the gospel in their own tongue at Pentecost begins “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites” — the latter days come, and the captivity of Elam brought again in the only way that lasts.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) treats Elam under sacred geography as the country of the Elamites, east of Babylonia, named from Elam the son of Shem, and identified with Elymais or Susiana.

expand to see more

ELAM, n. The eldest son of Shem, and the country peopled by his posterity.

It lay east of Babylonia and north of the Persian gulf, and is called by the ancients Elymais or Susiana.

Shushan, the palace of the Persian kings, stood in the province of Elam.

The Elamites were famed as archers, and are so described by Isaiah and Jeremiah.

Elamites were among those present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.

Key Scripture

Gen 14:1 — "And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;"

Isa 22:6 — "And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield."

Jer 49:35 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might."

Jer 49:39 — "But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The oracles against the nations are read as nationalist invective; Elam ends in a promise of restoration, which shows the judgments were never merely tribal curses.

expand to see more

The prophetic oracles against foreign nations are routinely characterised as the resentment of a small people versified. Elam refutes the characterisation in four verses. The judgment is severe — the bow broken, the people scattered to the four winds, the throne of the LORD set in Elam — and then, without a change of speaker, comes Jer 49:39 and the captivity brought again in the latter days. Egypt receives the same treatment (Jer 46:26), and Moab (Jer 48:47), and Ammon (Jer 49:6). A nationalist would not write that. The oracles are the judgments of the God of all the earth, and judgment in His hand has always had a door in it.

The second thing to name is how the promise was kept. Not by a restored Elamite kingdom — Elam never returned as a power — but by Elamites standing in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost hearing the wonderful works of God in their own tongue, and by the church that spread eastward through those provinces in the following centuries. The prophets speak of nations, and the fulfilment comes in a kingdom “out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9). Reading the oracles without that ending leaves them looking like grudges; reading them with it shows what they always were.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Eylam (H5867), Elam; qesheth (H7198), a bow; Greek Elamites (G1639).

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Eylam (H5867) — Elam; the son of Shem and the nation of his posterity (Gen 10:22).

Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; “the chief of their might”, the thing God says He will break.

Hebrew Kedorla'omer (H3540) — Chedorlaomer, the Elamite overlord of Gen 14.

Hebrew shub shebuth (H7725 + H7622) — to bring again the captivity; the formula of restoration in Jer 49:39.

Greek Elamites (G1639) — Elamites; named at Pentecost among the hearers (Act 2:9).

Usage

"“Chedorlaomer king of Elam” — the invasion that made Abram a rescuer."

"“I will break the bow of Elam” — judgment aimed at a nation's strength."

"“I will bring again the captivity of Elam” — a door left open in the sentence."
